Double-sided auctions, prevalent in financial markets, facilitate the exchange of goods between buyers and sellers. This research introduces a formal semantic framework for such auctions, subjecting the critical functionalities—specifically price of stability and market clearing—to rigorous deductive reasoning. The team implemented this approach within the Isabelle/HOL proof assistant, producing the first formally verified algorithm for double-sided matching. Its utility was demonstrated by validating results in commercial trading for electricity and securities.

This work examines the mass spectrum and decay constants of $FW$ bottom mesons within the Heavy Quark Effective Theory (HQET) framework. By employing the meson mass relation inherent in HQET alongside the decay constant formulation, we determine these parameters. Our analysis further investigates the influence of various quark condensates on both the mass spectrum and decay constants.

A line $ L $ in $ \mathbb{R}^n $ is termed nonexpansive if the distance between any two points on it never increases under projection; equivalently, every such line admits a periodic decomposition where the period function is monotone nonincreasing. This paper investigates the interplay between periodic decompositions and nonexpansive lines within the context of convex geometry.

Dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) serves as a widely adopted method for extracting dynamic characteristics from high-dimensional data, yet it struggles with robustness when applied to noisy environments. This study introduces a new approach to address these limitations by integrating kernel methods into the DMD framework. We demonstrate that this integration enables the separation of noise from meaningful signal data, particularly in scenarios where noise magnitude is substantial. The proposed method extends the capabilities of DMD to effectively analyze complex nonlinear systems.

This study examines the evolution of chess openings by analyzing a dataset of 11.5 million games from Lichess, an online chess platform. We introduce a methodology for assessing the intricacy of specific opening lines and for gauging the resemblance between distinct openings. Our analysis reveals that games adhering to established named openings exhibit greater move complexity than those utilizing unstructured sequences. Additionally, we observe a shift in Lichess data over time, marked by increased move complexity and a heightened similarity among various openings.

Although millisecond pulsars (MSPs) are widely recognized for their extreme magnetic fields and rapid spin, the mechanisms behind their formation and evolution remain poorly understood. This study investigates the evolutionary pathways of MSPs by analyzing the White Dwarf (WD) remnants of their progenitor systems. We examined the White Dwarfs in the PSR B1937+21 system and the MSP J0437−4715, which share the same pulsar, to determine their masses and radii. Our findings indicate that both WDs are nearly identical in mass and radius, with no significant differences detected. Consequently, we propose that both stars originated from a single progenitor star that split into two components via mass transfer. Furthermore, we estimated the mass of the common progenitor to be approximately 2.5 solar masses. This research offers a novel perspective on the evolutionary history of MSPs and provides a fresh avenue for investigating these objects.

We introduce a generalization of conserved quantities within Lagrangian frameworks for equations of any-order differential form, extending the approach originally developed for second-order systems by P. C. C. Papapetrou. This method integrates both space and temporal nonlocal elements. The current work formalizes Papapetrou's strategy within Lagrangian theory for arbitrary order $n$ and demonstrates its validity through the application to Eddington's variational principle for $n$-th order scalar field equations.

This study introduces a new method for shape retrieval, converting user sketches into 3D models to facilitate the acquisition of a personalized sketch database. We present the VR-Sketch2020 dataset, the first of its kind, comprising freeform sketches rendered in virtual reality by non-expert users. We also propose the SHAPESketch2020 engine, designed for a 3D environment to search and retrieve this database. We evaluate the system's performance using the SHAPESketch2020 engine across the VR-Sketch2020 and the newly introduced VR-Sketch2021 datasets.

We introduce a methodology for determining the precise orbital parameters of exoplanets by synchronizing observations from a global network of telescopes. This approach allows for the simultaneous tracking of the same planetary transit across multiple sites, thereby enhancing the accuracy of derived orbital elements. We demonstrate this technique by analyzing the highly eccentric exoplanet HD 80606 b, utilizing a dataset of 12 observations collected between 2016 and 2018. Our analysis reveals that the current ephemeris for HD 80606 b is insufficiently accurate to guarantee the optimal scheduling of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). To achieve a 1% timing precision for future JWST observations, the orbital period must be refined to an accuracy of approximately 0.01 seconds. We outline the specific requirements for achieving this level of precision and suggest that a coordinated, global observing campaign is necessary to fulfill them.

This study investigates the gravitational collapse of a perfect fluid characterized by a linear equation of state ($P = (\gamma - 1)\rho$) and adiabatic expansion ($\dot{P}/\dot{\rho} = P/\rho$). We demonstrate that, under these conditions, the dynamics of collapse can be mapped onto a two-dimensional Liénard system. Our analysis reveals that while the collapse remains isentropic throughout, it does not necessarily preserve the adiabatic nature of individual fluid elements. We establish both necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of a viable collapse solution. Furthermore, we prove that if the collapse is not adiabatic, it cannot maintain spherical symmetry. Our findings are illustrated through several examples, including perfect dust ($\gamma = 1$) and stiff matter ($\gamma = 2$).

This study employs the Iyer-Wald framework to derive modified versions of the Kerr and Reissner-Nordström black hole entropy and extremality conditions, incorporating effects from an arbitrary Lagrangian-Boundary Term (LBT). The black hole entropy is formulated via the integral of the Noether charge associated with an event horizon's bifurcation sphere and the corresponding Killing horizon, while the extremality criterion arises from balancing entropic change against variations in mass, charge, and angular momentum. Notably, the derived entropy aligns with results obtained using Wald's method in Semantics General Relativity, except when the Euler characteristic of the bifurcation sphere is not equal to one; in such instances, the LBT induces a distinct contribution to the Euler term. Furthermore, the derived extremality criteria accurately reflect adjustments to mass, electric charge, and rotational energy.

While reinforcement learning has demonstrated significant potential in end-to-end learning for robotic manipulation, its sample inefficiency remains a critical barrier to practical deployment. We introduce a novel anisotropic exploration drive for the end-effector, grounded in the concept of mechanical impedance, to enhance learning sample utility. By optimizing the Jacobian Jacobian Jacobian's singular values through this approach, we ensure the exploration strategy is most effective within the task's critical manifold. Empirical results across multiple tasks demonstrate that our method outperforms standard baseline exploration strategies.

We introduce an extended "colourful" Poincaré symmetry, which incorporates the standard Poincaré group alongside an $SU(N)$ internal symmetry. Associated with this symmetry is a unique set of massless mass-carrying massless particles, which possess a characteristic mass function that varies with the $SU(N)$ representation. We demonstrate that these mass functions obey specific differential equations, which are resolved to yield explicit forms for the corresponding masses. Furthermore, we construct the action terms for both field theories and mechanics governed by this "colourful" Poincaré framework. These masses are subsequently expressed in terms of the $SU(N)$ Casimir operators. Finally, we explore the implications of this extended symmetry for theories of gravity and Yang-Mills dynamics.

We present new parameterized algorithms addressing the fundamental problem of determining whether a directed acyclic graph supports an upward planar representation. Our approach achieves a $2^k\cdot\textsf{poly}(n)$ running time, where $k$ denotes the graph's upward planarity defect and $n$ is the total number of vertices. This defect measures the minimum count of edges that must be removed to render the graph upward planar. Our methodology extends existing exact linear-time techniques for recognizing upward planarity by adapting them for the parameterized context. Specifically, we define and employ a refined graph minor known as the upward platoid, which serves as a more suitable alternative to the standard platoid used in prior related work.

Current methods for navigation within images typically rely on an external memory network to store a fixed number of past observations, which are subsequently retrieved to enhance the agent's forwarder. However, this approach suffers from inefficiency because it stores every single memory regardless of relevance, potentially leading to redundant information. To address this limitation, we introduce **MemoNav**, a novel hierarchical architecture designed to selectively retain only informative memories. In this system, a gate mechanism determines whether to incorporate the latest observation into the memory based on its potential utility. Furthermore, to ensure effective retrieval, we employ a hierarchical organization of stored memories alongside an attention-based mechanism for their selection. Extensive testing across the navigation tasks demonstrates that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques.

The advent of 4G LTE networks, designed to support mobile broadband, introduced the Small Cell (SC) concept, which has since become integral to mobile networks through 4G, 5G, and the emerging 6G standards. This paper examines the evolution of LTE-based SCs across generations, analyzing their historical development, current status, and future trajectory. It explores the role of SCs in enhancing 6G performance, focusing on key advancements such as AI/ML integration, network slicing, and the NEMU architecture. Additionally, the study addresses upcoming challenges in the SC domain, including AI/ machine learning applications, security and privacy measures, and the implementation of 6G New Radio (NR) for Small Cells.

This work introduces a new framework modeling complex systems as weighted, directed hypergraphs, where an edge signifies that source nodes exert control over a target node. We establish the existence of canonical dynamics within this setting and investigate their fundamental properties, specifically addressing continuity, topological conjugacy, existence of solutions across all timeframes, and invariance under symmetries. Additionally, we examine specific applications, ranging from multi-agent systems to biological networks.

We introduce a method for quantifying the entanglement growth of time-evolved local operators and examine its behavior under chaotic and integrable dynamics. By introducing and analyzing the von Neumann entanglement entropy derived from the operator's eigen-decomposition, we demonstrate that while typical operators follow similar entanglement profiles to many-body states, those commuting with a conserved quantity exhibit markedly different behavior. We further investigate the universality of this entanglement entrop y, showing its dependence on the operator norm and support size, and utilize these findings to suggest a framework for reconstructing quasi-local conserved charges in isolated quantum systems.

The 7.47 MeV state in 12C, known as the Hoyle state, is a resonance of extreme significance for explaining cosmic carbon nucleosynthesis. Its total width is approximately 8.6 eV, with a direct-decay component of roughly 3.0 eV attributed to alpha emission from an 8Li intermediate state, while the remainder arises predominantly from photon emission. This study presents a direct, medium-insensitive measurement of the direct-decay fraction using the Gran Sasso Alpha-Beta experiment, yielding a result of (3.0 ± 0.4 ± 0.4) eV. This new determination aligns with previous findings but achieves superior precision, with an overall relative uncertainty of 13%.

This study employs a phase-field framework to investigate dynamic crack propagation in two dimensions, utilizing a moving boundary condition that enforces zero energy flux at the crack tip. By varying parameters with dimensions of length and time, we map the conditions under which oscillatory modes emerge, characterized by an amplitude growing along the fracture path and a radius of oscillation that expands progressively. While these simulations exhibit a singular stress field at the crack tip, they demonstrate that the crack-tip morphology is highly sensitive to the Intrinsic material length scale, which dictates both oscillation amplitude and curvature. Furthermore, we document a transition from these oscillatory patterns to a tip-splitting instability, wherein the crack bifurcates into two parallel paths. This bifurcation is driven by a non-singular, quasi-static stress distribution at the tip, a phenomenon that arises specifically when the system's time scale is sufficiently extended.

This study examines finite-state channels (FSCs) with feedback, where the system state is accessible to the encoder. It establishes that for any such channel, the capacity $C_{\rm FB}$ surpasses the forward capacity $C$, which denotes the rate achievable without feedback. The paper derives an upper bound, labeled $\overline{C}_{\rm FB}$, and demonstrates that this bound is tight for specific channel scenarios. Additionally, it proposes a computable lower bound, denoted as $\underline{C}_{\rm FB}$, which effectively approximates capacity in many cases.

We investigate the attractive Rashba Hubbard model featuring spin-singlet superconductivity, employing both mean-field theory and dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT). Our findings reveal that, contrary to expectations, the system does not exhibit a transition to a topological superconducting phase characterized by a spin-triplet state or a p-wave pairing symmetry. Instead, a spin-singlet topological superconducting phase emerges directly from the attractive short-range interaction, a state that persists across all values of the Rashba coupling. This phase is confirmed through the analysis of the superconducting gap structure, pairing order parameters, and the density of states. Furthermore, the spin susceptibility and the momentum-resolved spectral function offer significant insights into the nature of the pairing mechanism and the defining features of this topological superconducting state.

This paper outlines the submissions made by the UvA-Center for AI and Medicine (UvA-CAIM) for SemEval-2021 Task 9 (SEM-TAB-FACTS). Our team addressed two sub-tasks: Table Retrieval and Table Verification. For Table Retrieval, we utilized a single-stage retrieval approach, whereas our Table Verification system combined evidence extraction from both text and tables with large language models (LLMs) and an ensemble of classifiers. These models were trained using a synthetic dataset generated via GPT-3. Our methods achieved first place in both sub-tasks on the development set and second place on the test set.

This paper examines the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics. We outline two primary rationales for their necessity: first, ensuring that probability densities remain real-valued, and second, that probability amplitudes allow for meaningful interference. To illustrate the latter, we present a simplified model of the double-slit experiment. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating complex numbers into the formalism enables the derivation of an irreversible evolution equation from reversible unitary dynamics, thereby accounting for irreversibility in damped phenomena.

For a graph $G$, the distance $d_G(u,v)$ represents the length of the shortest path between vertices $u$ and $v$. A subset $S \subseteq V(G)$ has a metric dimension $\gamma(G)$ if there exists no other such subset of the same cardinality for which the distance between any pair of vertices is uniquely determined; specifically, for distinct vertices $u$ and $v$, $d_G(u,w)$ differs within $S$. This paper introduces and examines the concept of truncated metric dimension, denoted as $\gamma_k(G)$, which considers only the first $k$ edges of paths rather than the entire distance. We establish several properties regarding this new measure for various graphs, including determining its values for specific families like cycles and providing a polynomial algorithm to determine $\gamma_k(G)$.

A set of differential equations representing long-range (LRF) and radial (RPF) flows are derived. The ground surface is modeled as a sharp interface between saturated and unsaturated zones, with the water table height defined as the interface's vertical coordinate. The system is governed by the Darcy-Forchheimer law, Darcy's law, and the continuity equation. The model incorporates the full nonlinear relationship between water content and matric potential alongside the complete Brooks-Corey hydraulic conductivity function. The water table's temporal evolution is described by a second-order, fully nonlinear, fully coupled hyperbolic partial differential equation. The study examines the water table dynamics in both finite and unbounded domains, analyzing the impacts of well discharge, initial water content, saturated depth, and Brooks-Corey parameters. The derived equations are solved numerically using the finite difference method. The model's validity is confirmed through comparisons with published numerical and analytical solutions found in the literature.

This study investigates the potential of integrating ozone and ultraviolet (UV) radiation to oxidize sulfur dioxide (SO₂) into sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) within the gas phase, specifically targeting flue gas from coal-fired power plants. The research evaluates the reaction kinetics of SO₂ oxidation by ozone and the influence of UV radiation on these rates, utilizing a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model. The analysis indicates that the combined application of ozone and UV light offers a more energy-efficient approach for removing SO₂ compared to using ozone alone.

This paper introduces an open-source, transaction-level simulation environment for general neuromorphic processors, designed to enable the rapid prototyping of algorithms and software. This transaction-level approach facilitates efficient communication between a processor and its peripheral components, such as memory and sensors. The environment is extensible, allowing researchers to integrate various abstract hardware components. Developed as an SystemC-based Virtual Platform, it operates in parallel with actual hardware, making it ideal for use with Instruction Set Emulators and the Instruction Set Software Development Kits. The platform's flexibility supports the simulation of diverse architectures, ranging from RISC-V to dedicated, architecture-specific neuromorphic designs.

Recent breakthroughs in neural reasoning have enabled the end-to-end training of models capable of solving complex tasks requiring multi-step logical deduction. However, these approaches currently fall short in handling the kind of open-world uncertainty that defines real-world scenarios. This study introduces a method for decision tree learning adapted to argumentation frameworks, specifically those containing quantifiers such as "all" or "some." Our framework treats the construction of these trees as a synthesis problem, aiming to derive rules that are both logically sound and maximally general. We formalized this approach within a deep learning context, creating a neural architecture capable of ingressing premises and quantitative confidence levels to output an indecision tree representing the final conclusion. Empirical evaluations confirm that this method not only matches the deductive performance of standard baseline algorithms but also provides human-interpretable justifications for its decisions.

The Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) algorithm is widely recognized for its effectiveness in measuring the similarity between time series, yet its computational complexity scales quadratically with sequence lengths, rendering it impractical for comparing long series. While various techniques have been developed to mitigate this issue, they often fail to deliver consistent speedups. This paper introduces PrunedDTW, a method capable of achieving a speedup factor of up to 100 compared to standard DTW. Crucially, PrunedDTW retains the ability to compute the exact distance without approximation. Additionally, we demonstrate how to integrate Early Abandoning into PrunedDTW to further accelerate a similarity search. Experimental results confirm that this proposed approach outperforms existing solutions by a significant margin.

Testing represents a critical component of the software development lifecycle, yet current research indicates that students often struggle to acquire the necessary testing competencies through conventional instruction. This study introduces and evaluates an inquiry-based teaching approach designed to foster these skills, specifically examining whether it surpasses traditional teaching methods in effectiveness. The study further investigates the comparative value of two types of feedback provided during problem-solving: conceptual, high-level guidance versus detailed, low-level information. Empirical data gathered from 120 undergraduate participants across three distinct conditions revealed that the condition utilizing detailed feedback yielded the most positive outcomes for student performance.

Explainable AI (XAI) has become a critical area of research as Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) increasingly replace traditional models in complex domains like medical diagnosis and autonomous driving. While many existing methods focus on generating local explanations for specific predictions, there is a growing need for global insights that clarify a model's behavior across entire input spaces. This paper introduces an innovative ILP-based framework capable of providing comprehensive explanations for DNNs. By integrating concept learning with linear programming, our approach derives both the input features and the architectural parameters of a simplified proxy model that mimics the original network's logic. We evaluate this methodology on two distinct tasks: explaining a standard CNN used for image classification and analyzing a complex, non-linearly separable GNN.

Over-smoothing stands as a recognized limitation of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), resulting in a scenario where increasing the number of convolutional layers causes distinct graph nodes to approach identical feature representations, ultimately causing network training failure. This paper introduces a novel layer-wise analysis method to examine how this effect emerges during training. The investigation reveals that over-smoothing is not uniform across all nodes or layers but is instead governed by the interplay between a node's degree and the convolutional mode of the specific GCN layer. Crucially, we discovered that an exponential relationship exists between a node's degree and its corresponding smoothing rate. Based on these findings, we propose a new model termed Degree-Convolution that effectively mitigates over-smoothing. Empirical evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate that integrating this degree-based convolution into existing GCNs significantly boosts performance.

This study presents the latest search results for dark matter particles generated alongside Z bosons during proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, operating at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. Data collected by the CMS experiment from 2016 to 2018 span an integrated luminosity of 137 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis examines final states containing exactly one isolated lepton (either an electron or a muon) and significant missing transverse momentum. Constraints on the cross-section for processes involving a single visible particle and invisible particles are established across various transverse momentum spectra. These findings are interpreted within the framework of simplified models, specifically focusing on vector and axial-vector Z-mediated interactions as well as Higgs-mediated production. Furthermore, exclusion limits are derived for the parameter spaces of various dark matter models, including those based on a real singlet scalar, complex scalar, and fermion dark matter candidates.

A topological group equipped with socks is a $T_{0}$-space where every point is the intersection of all its open neighborhoods that form a commutative group under the space's uniformity. This class includes all completely uniform groups. We demonstrate that the long colimit of a functor mapping topological groups to such spaces (long to be precise: directed colimit) remains a topological group with socks. Furthermore, we show that any $T_{0}$-space with socks can be realized as the long colimit of an increasing sequence of complete uniform groups. Finally, we prove that the long colimit of an arbitrary directed system of topological groups with socks is equivalent to the long colimit of an ascending chain of completely uniform groups.

Remote epitaxy enables the growth of high-quality crystals on substrates that are not in direct thermal contact with them, yet it often suffers from limited control over nucleation and the resulting film morphology. This study investigates the remote epitaxial growth of the Heusler alloy Co$_2$MnSb on a graphene/sapphire system, where the insulating graphene layer allows the sapphire crystal to influence the film's structure. By adjusting the distance between the source and the substrate, we successfully induce a transition in growth modes, shifting from Co$_2$MnSb pinhole coverage at short distances to a remote mode at larger separations. This versatility allows for the engineering of diverse nanostructures, ranging from isolated nanodots to continuous layers, nanowires, and moiré superlattices. Furthermore, we analyze the growth mechanisms behind these patterns and examine the electronic properties of the resulting Co$_2$MnSb films.

This paper introduces a multivariate time series model designed to capture both heteroscedasticity and trends within the first-order autoregressive framework, alongside a forecasting method. We demonstrate that the maximum likelihood estimators for this model converge at a rate of $O(n^{-2/3})$ and exhibit asymptotic non-Gaussian stability. Our analysis further establishes the consistency of the forecasting estimator before applying the model to simulate data and evaluate its performance through numerical experiments.

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has observed the massive galaxy cluster ACT-CL J0102$-$4915, also known as "El Gordo," a system renowned for its recent, high-energy collision. This study presents the initial JWST Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) data for the field, which reveals a red supergiant (RSG) located 1.2 arcseconds from the cluster's center. This star, identified as a lensed object, exhibits a magnification of $\mu=1.5\pm0.2$ and a flux amplification of $\mu_{\rm F}=2.1\pm0.3$. We have developed a new lens model that incorporates the NIRCam data, yielding a refined redshift estimate of $z=0.380\pm0.004$ for the progenitor. This discovery marks the first confirmed RSG at a cosmological distance ($z>0.3$) identified by JWST. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the original Hubble Space Telescope (HST) data, which previously identified this source as a foreground Galactic star, was likely affected by a systematic error.

This study introduces a collaborative profit-sharing framework between a content provider (CP) and a network service provider (ISP) to incentivize the ISP to enhance its network quality. The ISP, which operates as a monopolist, allocates resources to a single ISP facing demand from a CP that possesses only partial knowledge of this resource allocation. The CP's objective is to design an optimal sharing contract that maximizes its own profit. The analysis reveals that the optimal contract takes the form of a linear revenue-sharing agreement. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that implementing such sharing arrangements benefits both parties, although the ISP gains more significantly than the CP.

This work presents an adjunction where the left-hand functor constructs a Hilbert space from observables using a state, while the right-hand functor derives observables and states from a given Hilbert space. This structure forms a correspondence akin to a 2-categorical adjunction, enabling the derivation of algebraic observables via universal properties. Specifically, this approach recovers the commutant relations of the Wightman two-point function and extends these concepts to arbitrary even-point correlation functions.

$\alpha$-attractor models have become a prominent area of study within inflation theory, largely due to their ability to generate viable scenarios that easily satisfy the requisite conditions for slow-roll inflation. This review offers a comprehensive analysis of the fundamental properties and model variants of these $\alpha$-attractors, specifically examining how different metric formulations influence the predictions of the universe's primordial perturbations. We further detail the methodology for calculating the critical parameters of the slow-roll regime and the resulting predictions for inflationary observables, culminating in a detailed comparison of model-specific predictions against observational data from the Planck mission.

This paper demonstrates that for a real-analytic Fuchsian surface embedded in $S^3$, there exists a neighborhood within the quasi-Fuchsian region of the corresponding real-analytic family where the measured laminations at infinity of the manifold form a real-analytic foliation. This result stands as an analytic counterpart to Minsky's real-analytic structural theorem.

This study examines the distribution of cross-sectional portfolio returns, which we term the "portfolio return distribution." Utilizing data from the CRSP/Compustat merged dataset, we demonstrate that this distribution exhibits significant skewness and kurtosis, a pattern that remains stable over time and persists even when excluding small-cap stocks. We further explore the implications of these distributional characteristics on the moments of cross-sectional return variance and reveal a positive correlation between skewness/kurtosis and CRPS variance. Consequently, standard errors derived under the assumption of normally distributed returns are notably smaller than those calculated using heteroskedasticity-robust methods, leading to inflated t-statistics. By integrating this approach with the factor models of Fama and French (1992) and Carhart (1997), we observe a marked increase in the statistical significance of momentum and size factors, alongside a reduction in the average cross-sectional return variance for portfolios constructed from industry- and size-matched pairs.

This study introduces a classification framework for heart sounds designed to detect murmurs by leveraging deep learning techniques. The methodology utilizes a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) trained on the MIT/BIH Arrhythmia Database, which consists of stethoscope-recorded heart sounds. The network was trained using two distinct data augmentation strategies: 1) adding Gaussian white noise to simulate environmental background noise, and 2) applying a 1D convolutional filter to emulate the frequency response characteristics of varying stethoscope types. The model was evaluated on a test set comprising 100 previously unseen heart sound signals. The results demonstrated that training with the stethoscope response simulation yielded superior performance, achieving an accuracy of 88%, an error rate of 12%, and an F1 score of 87.5%.

We address the concerns raised by Czarnecki et al. regarding our recent study on atomic parity violation in cesium. Our analysis demonstrates that the majority of the four-point contributions to the two-photon- one-electron parity-odd amplitude can be expressed via a limited set of nuclear matrix elements, which are capable of being extracted from existing beta decay and muon-capture data. Consequently, we reaffirm our original conclusion regarding the stringent limits on the CP-violating electron-nucleon interaction derived.

A twist serves as a local system's cohomology calculation for tori, defined by its orientation-preserving or reversing homeomorphism. This paper determines tori equivantly these cohomologies, specifically under actions by the seven 2-dimensional crystallographic point groups.

This project addresses the urgent challenge of global warming by integrating mathematical modeling with computer science. It involves two core components: a model that predicts how carbon dioxide levels influence the Earth's albedo and temperature, and a collaborative platform that allows users to modify the code, execute simulations, and share their outcomes.

This study presents a detailed investigation into the boundedness and the $H^1$-algebra status of the series operator, $\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{b_n}} T_n$, defined over the series of modified Riesz transforms on the modified discrete array $a^{(1/2)}_{\mathbb{Z}_+}$. The analysis further explores how the underlying modified Riesz potentials influence the structural properties of these operators when applied to modified discrete Hardy spaces and characterizes the series operators that reside within an $H^1$-algebra of the modified Riesz potentials.

This study employs a between-subjects experimental design to assess how credibility influences bidding behavior in second-price auctions. Participants were divided into two groups: one engaged in standard auctions, while the other played under a "pledged" condition where bidders submitted commitment pledges to specific bidding ranges. Although the covering letter was signed by the principal rather than the individual bidder, both conditions shared identical financial incentives. Results indicate that the pledge significantly increased bid credibility, causing pledging bidders to approach first-price auction outcomes more closely than those in the control group. Furthermore, the principal observed a substantial rise in their own bids within the credibly committed environment, a trend mirrored in the final auction revenues.

This study investigates the evolution of the locally rotationally symmetric (LRS) Bianchi-I cosmological model within the framework of $f(Q)$-gravitational theory, which offers a teleparallel equivalent to modified gravity based on the symmetric gauge potential. We derive exact solutions for the LRS Bianchi-I model and demonstrate that the specific choice of the functional form for $g(\mathcal{Q})$ and the associated boundary conditions directly influences the resulting cosmic evolution. Our findings indicate that the model undergoes isotropization as the universe transitions from an initial singularity, a behavior consistent with the standard $\Lambda$CDM paradigm.

We establish a Gr\"obner basis for the ideal defining the nullcone of $B$ within $GL_n$, where $n$ is a positive integer and $B$ denotes the group of upper-triangular matrices; this basis consists of determinants of specific submatrices formed by columns indexed as powers of two and rows indexed as arithmetic progressions. This result enables the computation of the Hilbert polynomial for the variety $\mathcal{X}_r$, representing the regular nilpotent Hessenberg variety associated with a partition $h=(n-r,1,\dots,1)$ for any $1 \leq r \leq n$. Furthermore, we prove that $\mathcal{X}_r$ admits a geometric vertex decomposition, a finding that facilitates the demonstration of an explicit Frobenius splitting for $\mathcal{X}_r$ applicable to all positive characteristic fields.

Neural Painters are generative models designed to create art by learning from the works of specific historical painters. This research explores the capabilities of these systems by analyzing how they internalize and replicate the stylistic traits of their training data. We evaluate the Neural Painters of Rembrandt, Van Gogh, and Picasso, demonstrating their proficiency in mimicking key characteristics such as brushstroke textures, chromatic palettes, and the application of light and shadow. Furthermore, we investigate the practical utility of these models in aiding human artists, specifically through collaborative workflows that integrate human input with neural generation.

We propose a new model featuring vector-like quarks to address the observed flavor anomalies in both $B$ and $p$ meson decays. This framework offers a unified explanation for the specific branching ratios and angular distributions reported by the LHCb collaboration, specifically the $B$ meson decays ($B_0\to\phi K^0$, $B_0\to\phi K^0_s$, $B_0\to\phi K^0_{L}$) and the $B$ meson decays ($B^+\to K^+\mu^+\mu^-$, $B^+\to K^+\mu^+\mu^-$). Our approach simultaneously accounts for the flavor anomalies in $B$ and $p$ meson decays, specifically the $B$ meson decays ($B^+\to K^+\mu^+\mu^-$, $B^+\to K^+\mu^+\mu^-$) and the $B$ meson decays ($B^+\to K^+\mu^+\mu^-$, $B^+\to K^+\mu^+\mu^-$). This approach provides a coherent explanation for the flavor anomalies in $B$ and $p$ meson decays, specifically the $B$ meson decays ($B^+\to K^+\mu^+\mu^-$, $B^+\to K^+\mu^+\mu^-$

This paper introduces OpenQuestion, an open-source collection of 10,000 information-seeking queries drawn from academic papers. For each query, we provide multiple turns of a dialogue, where each turn includes a question, a set of relevant research papers, and excerpts from those papers that address the inquiry. We also include human-verified answers for every single query. To support the development and evaluation of academic question-answering systems, we have created several specialized subsets and benchmark tasks.

In this study, we examine fast neutrino flavor instabilities within the context of axisymmetric and fully three-dimensional core-collapse supernova models. Our findings reveal that these fast instabilities persist in the post-shock region, characterized by spatial scales of approximately $10$ km, existing alongside the more commonly known collective neutrino oscillations. While the post-shock zone exhibits a low density of lepton number, we observe that the instability strength is governed by the average occupation numbers of antineutrinos and neutrinos, rather than relying on the depletion of Pauli blocking. Additionally, we analyzed the influence of matter effects on these instabilities and determined that they remain viable in the post-shock area, provided the electron density does not surpass $10^{11}$ cm$^{-3}$.

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent pediatric condition characterized by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Although current diagnostic methods rely on subjective clinical observations, they often face challenges with bias and low reliability. Consequently, researchers have turned to neuroimaging technologies to explore potential diagnostic biomarkers. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to identify critical brain regions in resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data for improved ADHD diagnosis. The framework employs a dual mechanism: first, it utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract features from 3D structural MRI data; second, it applies an attention module to weigh the significance of these features across different brain regions. This approach not only enhances diagnostic accuracy but also offers interpretable insights into which brain areas drive the model's decisions. Experimental validation using the publicly available ADHD200 dataset demonstrated that the proposed method achieved an 84.1% accuracy rate, surpassing existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This paper introduces a discrete-time epidemic SISi model, where the final 'i' denotes infectiousness. In this framework, susceptible individuals may transition to an infectious state that alters how they interact with others, thereby modifying the infection risk for potential contacts. We present a next-generation matrix approach to determine the basic reproduction number for this discrete-time SISi framework. Additionally, we analyze the global asymptotic stability of both disease-free and endemic equilibrium points.

Acronyms are ubiquitous in the medical domain, where a single term may possess multiple definitions contingent upon the specific clinical context. For instance, "COPD" refers to "Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease" in a hospital setting but could denote "Congenital Ovarian Peritoneal Disease" in gynecological literature. Resolving these contextual ambiguities is vital for advancing Natural Language Processing (NNDL) applications in medicine, such as clinical decision support and the extraction of insights from medical records. This paper introduces "MadDog," a novel web-based platform designed to identify acronyms and generate or retrieve the appropriate definitions based on textual context. The system employs a two-stage methodology: first, it utilizes a context-independent model to detect acronyms within a text, followed by a context-dependent model that provides the specific meaning aligned with that textual environment.

This study introduces a novel mechanism for thermoelectric switching and rectification within devices operating under quantum Hall conditions. We examine a setup comprising two quantum point contacts connected to three non-magnetic quantum Hall edges, where the system's response to both heat and charge currents is analyzed using a non-equilibrium Keldysh framework. Our analysis demonstrates that, in the absence of magnetic fields, the presence of interference patterns in the system's topology enables the complete switching of both charge and heat fluxes. We further investigate the impact of applying a magnetic field, which induces a Hall deflection in the system's electronic trajectories. This results in distinct behaviors for charge and heat transport, including the capability to rectify temperature gradients and convert them into unidirectional currents.

DNA storage offers a promising avenue for addressing the escalating demand for data storage capacity and computational power. Although encoding data at the single-molecule level theoretically allows for vast storage density, current practical implementations typically rely on storing individual strands within microtiter plate wells, where each molecule represents a single record. This paper introduces a novel data structure designed to optimize DNA storage by establishing a hierarchy among strands within a well, thereby enhancing access efficiency. Furthermore, we introduce update mechanisms that enable specific hierarchy modifications without necessitating the complete rewrite of an entire well's data. Experimental results indicate that our approach achieves a 100-fold improvement in both storage density and operational efficiency compared to existing methods.

Recent years have seen significant research into topological insulators and semimetals, driven by the striking presence of nodal lines in their band structures. This article examines the topological character of these lines and explores their implications for the group velocity of electrons moving near Fermi level. Furthermore, we outline a method for calculating the Neron-Neumann contribution to the anomalous Hall effect, which serves as a robust topological indicator. The discussion extends to the role of line nodes in systems lacking translational symmetry, presenting recent experimental results from topological insulators and Weyl semimetals. Finally, we highlight the novel developments in photonics, specifically the experimental realization of such lines within photonic crystals and coupled resonator arrays.

This study introduces a novel analytical technique for calculating the propagation velocity of traveling waves initiated by a point source pacemaker within an excitable medium governed by the Nagumo equations. This approach yields a closed-form expression that aligns closely with prior simulation and experimental findings. Furthermore, the work examines how propagation speed responds to variations in the source's activation duration and frequency, offering a theoretical framework that accurately predicts these effects, as confirmed by simulations.

This study introduces a subslinear-time quantum algorithm for approximating the von Neumann entropy of an arbitrary quantum state. We establish that estimating this entropy to additive error $\varepsilon$ can be achieved in $O(\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2}\log^2 d)$ quantum queries, where $d$ represents the system's dimension, $\delta$ denotes the desired statistical accuracy, and the statistical error is bounded by $\delta$.

Deep learning models demand extensive computational resources, particularly for training, which necessitates a cloud-based approach. This paper examines the various forms of AI infrastructure available in cloud environments, including the utilization of AI-specific services, pre-trained models, and open-source libraries. It further outlines the critical factors for architecting an effective AI data storage system and presents a proposed data workflow pipeline designed to support the entire lifecycle of AI development and deployment.

This study introduces a semi-self-supervised framework designed to automatically assign ICD codes for diagnosis and procedures. Utilizing two distinct semi-self-supervised pre-training phases, the model effectively leverages unlabelled clinical notes to enhance performance. Pre-training is conducted in these stages: first, it performs cross-encoder masking on ICD codes, followed by cross-encoder masking on clinical text. Subsequently, the framework is fine-tuned via distillation on top of pre-trained representations using labelled data. Experiments demonstrate that this approach significantly surpasses existing methods, achieving an F1 score of 64.1% on the 2018 version of the public ICUd-2018 dataset.

Let $R$ denote the polynomial ring with coefficients in a field $k$ and $I$ be a monomial ideal within $R$. This work investigates the properties of such ideals, specifically focusing on when they are nearly Cohen-Macaulay or possess linear resolutions.

Machine learning algorithms are essential for analyzing vast datasets to derive meaningful patterns and insights. This paper introduces novel quantum algorithms designed for both supervised and unsupervised learning, which are subsequently evaluated through quantum simulations. The proposed unsupervised method utilizes the quantum phase estimation technique to execute spectral decomposition, automatically identifying the latent structure within data. For the supervised approach, we employ a support vector machine variant that employs spectral decomposition to determine the optimal decision boundary. These algorithms are executed on the IBM quantum processor, and the results are compared against the IBM Q5 and Q6 systems to demonstrate their efficacy.

We present findings from the KMTNet Systematic Planetary Anomaly Search (KSPAS) for data collected in 2018. Utilizing a Bayesian inference method, we identified 10 planetary anomalies in the 2018 sample, bringing the total count of confirmed planetary anomalies discovered by KSPAS to 19. Of these 10 new candidates, 8 are located in the prime fields of the Milky Way's bulge, while the remaining two reside in the Magellanic Clouds. Our analysis indicates that 8 of the 10 new candidates are likely planetary-mass objects orbiting K-dwarf stars, whereas the other two appear to be stellar-mass companions orbiting low-mass stars.

Accurate light shadow computation is vital for both visual realism and performance in computer graphics, particularly within inverse problem frameworks like depth estimation and surface reconstruction. This study introduces a novel, differentiable approach for calculating shadows, prioritizing efficiency and effectiveness. We demonstrate that standard differentiable rendering methods can be enhanced to produce correct shadow cues with minimal additional computational overhead. Crucially, our method enables the differentiable simulation of complex occlusion scenarios involving multiple dynamic objects and a rigorous camera system.

This study introduces a probabilistic framework for estimating origin-destination (OD) demand, utilizing daily traffic datasets. By applying maximum likelihood estimation, OD flows are inferred from traffic counts recorded at specific links. The methodology accounts for the uncertainty inherent in these estimates, constructing confidence intervals to delineate probable demand ranges. The proposed model is validated using real-world data from the San Francisco Bay Area Freeway System.

We investigate the behavior of one-dimensional coupled oscillator networks, where each individual oscillator follows either the Van der Pol or Duffing equation, allowing for variations in natural frequencies and damping factors. Our analysis reveals that the final state of the synchronized array depends critically on the specific combination of damping and frequency values inherent to each oscillator. We identify two primary outcomes: a global phase-locking state, where all frequencies converge to a common frequency, and a coexistence state, characterized by the persistence of multiple stable attractors. Furthermore, we examine the conditions under which these states occur by analyzing the energy landscape of the system.

The paper demonstrates that the Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms exhibit transient equivalence, meaning they yield identical sequences of self-avoiding walks with near-identical success rates up to any fixed time $t$ as $n \to \infty$. This finding arises from the observation that both algorithms employ the same random walk and apply a depth-first search strategy, albeit with distinct criteria for determining tree inclusion. Consequently, these insights facilitate a two-phase approach for uniformly sampling spanning trees: first executing a standard random walk to the target node, followed by conditionally incorporating the resulting path into the tree based on a specific success metric.

This paper introduces the MusicTM-Dataset, a novel collection of trios comprising sheet music, lyrics, and corresponding music audio. We present the dataset and a deep learning framework designed to model the interconnections between these three modalities. Our proposed method utilizes a multi-modal transformer to extract representations from the sheet music, lyrics, and audio, employing a contrastive learning strategy to align these features within a shared latent space. We also developed a multi-task learning approach to enhance representation quality by integrating auxiliary audio and musical scores data. Experimental results demonstrate that the model effectively captures multi-modal relationships in the sheet music, lyrics, and audio, showing significant potential for applications such as music generation, transcription, and retrieval.

This study explores the potential of natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning (ML) techniques within the context of visual data exploration. We utilize ontodia, a flexible and adaptable framework for such exploration, in conjunction with Word2Vec embeddings derived from the NLP processing of Wikidata. By applying this combination to a subset of the Cambridge Information Database (CID), we illustrate how Word2Vec can effectively surface novel connections between entities. The paper concludes by discussing the advantages and constraints of this specific approach, alongside a forward-looking perspective on integrating further NLP and ML capabilities into visual data exploration.

This study examines the stability of black solitons within optical systems governed by an integrable nonlinear Schrödinger equation featuring intensity-dependent dispersion. The governing dynamics are described by the damped driven equation $\partial_x\psi +ik\psi+i\partial_{tt}\psi+i\gamma|\psi_t|^2=0$, where the dimensionless parameters represent the wavevector ($k$), group velocity dispersion ($\beta_G=1$), and the intensity-dependent dispersive coefficient ($\gamma$). By conducting a perturbative analysis, we demonstrate that black solitons remain stable against long-wave perturbations provided the wave is subluminal. The derived stability criterion, $\beta_G^{\text{eff}}<0$, indicates that the total dispersion must be negative. This result aligns with the established principle that stability relies on the dominance of self-dispersion over linear dispersion. The analytical predictions are corroborated by numerical simulations of the associated two-point boundary value problem.

In the era of big data, data visualization serves as an essential tool for exploring and comprehending intricate systems. Nevertheless, the sheer complexity of data and its underlying models often overwhelms human analysts, who consequently struggle to derive meaningful insights. To address this, researchers have proposed various guidance mechanisms designed to assist users in navigating visual spaces effectively. While these methods offer specific recommendations, they frequently lack a cohesive theoretical framework to systematically support the entire visual analytics workflow. This paper introduces "Lotte," an extensible guidance framework that structures support around the core tasks of visual analytics: selection, exploration, and understanding. Lotte offers three primary contributions: (1) a guidance framework grounded in task- and user-centered theories of visual analytics; (2) an implementation of Lotte built upon the VALE environment; and (3) a demonstration of its extensibility through three specific techniques—each tailored to facilitate user actions within distinct visual analytics scenarios.

Achieving robust plasma confinement in stellarators is essential for their potential viability as fusion devices, a stability that is established by the initial magnetic field. Consequently, generating fields that support several configurations allows for the selection of the optimal state for confinement. We present an optimization technique designed to integrate fields for multiple coil sets within a single calculation, thereby enhancing both computational efficiency and the flexibility to include various coil geometries. This approach is validated using a test case based on the Wendelstein 7-X design, demonstrating that the derived fields accurately reproduce target fields for all included magnetic configurations.

This study introduces a non-invasive technique utilizing rapid magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to map temperature distributions within gas-solid fixed beds. By applying the Arrhenius equation to a model reaction, temperature profiles were generated to validate the approach. These experimental results were then compared against a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation of the same fixed bed system. The research demonstrates that the proposed method offers significant potential for investigating heat and mass transfer mechanisms in gas-solid fixed beds.

Biomolecular condensates are liquid droplets formed through the phase separation of proteins and nucleic acids, a process essential for organizing the cell. This study investigates the self-assembly dynamics of such droplets when composed of multiple shared components. We developed a coarse-grained model based on a pairwise potential that captures the coexistence of two distinct phase boundaries, thereby enabling the formation of droplets containing various protein complexes. Our findings indicate that the spatial distribution of these complexes critically dictates droplet characteristics, including size and internal composition. Specifically, we demonstrate that clustering of proteins enhances the overall material stability of the resulting droplets. Additionally, we analyzed the kinetics of self-assembly and found that the internal mixing state of droplets is governed by the interplay between the concentration of protein complexes and their interaction strengths. Ultimately, this work provides a mechanistic framework for how complex, multi-component condensates form within the cellular environment.

This study examines the rotation of sunspots and magnetic transients within the active region NOAA 11429, which was monitored by the Hinode satellite during its decay phase. The rotational dynamics of individual sunspots were tracked using H$\alpha$ images from the Solar Optical Telescope (SOT), while magnetic transients were identified through high-cadence data from the X-ray Telescope (XRT). The analysis reveals that sunspot rotation speeds are not uniform; they vary based on the specific location within the active region. Furthermore, the study establishes a correlation between these rotational variations and magnetic transients, suggesting that the former can serve as a predictive indicator for the latter.

In the 1970s, the weak $b$-principle was formulated by Sullivan as a criterion to assess the existence of non-trivial cohomology classes. In this work, we explore its application to the cohomology of space forms and explore connections to the Mumford conjecture. Our findings demonstrate that for a manifold $M$ with the fundamental group $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathord{\cdot}t$ (where $p$ is a prime), the Mumford conjecture holds for all primes $q$ distinct from $p$. Additionally, we establish that the inclusion map from the classifying spaces of two such manifolds with isomorphic fundamental groups induces a rational isomorphism on their cohomology.

This study introduces a computational framework designed to solve the quasi-static mechanical behavior of the left ventricle, focusing on fiber-specific stress, strain, and volume changes resulting from myocardial activation. The finite element discretization of the constitutive model yields a nonlinear system of equations solved via a quasi-Newton approach, where performance relies heavily on the efficiency of the pre-conditioned solver. We evaluate various domain decomposition and multilevel strategies, demonstrating that a hybrid of the Schur complement method with algebraic multigrid significantly accelerates convergence for both finite element types—tetrahedral and hexahedral. Furthermore, the solver exhibits scalability across distributed memory environments, sustaining effective performance up to 16,384 cores when simulating a left ventricle with 1.2 billion degrees of freedom.

Social tagging systems allow users to collaboratively annotate web resources, a process that has been shown to enhance the quality and quantity of metadata generated. Despite this collaborative potential, little is known about the extent to which individuals actually leverage these features. This study investigates four key dimensions of collaboration within Citebase, a social tagging platform: reuse, temporal activity patterns, interest sharing, and direct cooperative behavior. The analysis reveals that users frequently reuse existing tags, with the average inter-tagging interval decreasing progressively over time. Additionally, most activity clusters around specific periods, indicating shared interests among participants. Finally, while direct collaboration remains rare, the data suggests that users who engage in social networking activities within the system are more likely to contribute tags.

This study introduces a compact acoustic metacell, fabricated via two-photon polymerization, designed to reflect sound waves with a phase shift of $-\pi$ at ultrasonic frequencies. Integrated into a functional metagrating, this unit cell operates effectively at frequencies of 200 kHz and beyond, corresponding to acoustic wavelengths as short as 3.4 mm in air. The device successfully generates a highly directive, tunable narrow acoustic beam, achieving a beamwidth of 10° at 200 kHz and a divergence of 18° at 200 kHz (note: divergence typically increases with frequency; at 800 kHz, the measured beamwidth contracts to 18°). The operational mechanism relies on the interaction between the incident wave and the standing wave formed within the polymer microcavity, a phenomenon governed by a resonant condition that can be precisely adjusted by varying the cavity dimensions. This approach offers a versatile pathway for engineering microacoustic components capable of manipulating high-frequency waves.

This paper investigates the asymptotic dynamics of the two-dimensional FENE dumbbell model for compressible fluids. We demonstrate that the long-term behavior of the 2-D compressible FENE dumbbell model mirrors that of the corresponding Navier-Stokes equations. Specifically, it is shown that the global strong solutions of the 2-D FENE dumbbell model converge exponentially to a constant equilibrium state when measured against the Navier-Stokes solutions, provided a sufficiently small initial gap exists.

The evolution of wireless communication is increasingly defined by the integration of Integrated Access and Browsing (IAB), a technology designed to enhance network capacity and coverage through node-to-node resource sharing. While current IAB relies on a network architecture where a donor base station manages all radio resources, the mobile IAB paradigm envisions mobile IAB donors (mIAB-Ds) and relay access units (mIAB-Us) operating independently within a cellular environment. This mobile approach offers significant advantages, including enhanced flexibility, superior coverage, and greater energy efficiency. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the research landscape surrounding mobile IAB, examining the specific challenges it faces and the proposed solutions. We outline the fundamental principles of IAB and its adaptation for mobile scenarios, analyze key performance metrics, and explore the critical issues regarding mobility management, resource allocation, and access control. Finally, the study identifies remaining hurdles and proposes potential avenues for future investigation in this field.

The performance of many optimization algorithms relies heavily on the tuning of their internal hyperparameters, a task that is often approached through trial and error or by borrowing values from other contexts. This study addresses the automated determination of hyperparameters for the $(\mu+\lambda)$ evolutionary algorithm through a two-phase process. Initially, a set of candidate values for each parameter is identified by analyzing published research and observing their usage frequencies. Subsequently, a global sensitivity analysis is employed to evaluate how variations in these candidate values influence the algorithm's results, specifically its ability to solve the OneMax and Trap problems. The findings indicate that current practices regarding the configuration of evolutionary algorithm parameters are not well-supported by empirical evidence, and that the specific values used frequently in literature do not necessarily yield superior outcomes.

This paper examines the wave equation within quantum mechanics, demonstrating that it can be derived from the classical action principle when the Hamiltonian is substituted with its matrix representation. We further elucidate the significance of the matrix form of the Hamiltonian, illustrating its origin through both the transformation of continuous variables into discrete ones and the application of the probabilistic interpretation of the wave function. Ultimately, we assert that the matrix formulation of the Hamiltonian is as fundamental to quantum mechanics as are Planck's constant and the uncertainty principle.

Life-long learning (L2) represents a critical yet challenging aspect of intelligence, defined by the ability to acquire, retain, and transfer knowledge across multiple tasks. While recent breakthroughs in this area have yielded robust generic representations and transferable skills, constructing a comprehensive testing framework remains difficult. This paper introduces L2Explorer, a novel artificial agent operating within a virtual 3D world designed to evaluate and compare L2 capabilities across diverse scenarios. To support the broader research community, we have made L2Explorer publicly available at https://github.com/uni-tuebingen-ri/L2Explorer.

Liger is a proposed high-contrast, high-resolution spectrograph at Keck Observatory, designed to investigate the atmospheres of exoplanets and the interstellar medium. Its instrument architecture comprises a single, elongated, dual-beam setup, where each channel utilizes a grism and a linear detector array. Operating in both near-infrared and near-ultraviolet modes, the instrument employs a single grism that can be repositioned to switch between these bands. This dual-channel configuration enables simultaneous observations, allowing for the cancellation of telluric absorption features and the isolation of Doppler-shifted planetary signals. To support these scientific goals, a specialized data reduction system has been developed. This system is built upon the IRAF package framework and integrates several key components: data ingestion, calibration, and analysis tools. The analysis module is further divided into two modes: one for standard observations and another for the specific Doppler spectroscopy required for Liger. This paper details the instrument's design and outlines the software interfaces and data reduction system.

This study introduces a novel class of time-independent, periodic, shear-driven flow solutions for the 2D Euler equation, termed "shear waves." These waves emerge from the vortex streets characteristic of 2D flow around a periodic array of obstacles in motion relative to one another. Although the velocity field exhibits vorticity, its streamfunction remains harmonic. The existence of these solutions was established via a fixed-point argument applied to the periodic setting, leveraging the observation that the Couette flow serves as an exact solution to the Helmhöfer-von Kármán (HVK) integral equation governing vortex street dynamics. The work further demonstrates that this 2D system serves as a sufficient condition for the validity of such flows within the broader 3D context of the Euler equations. Distinctly, unlike the stationary waves described by the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, these traveling waves feature both non-zero vorticity and a non-uniform amplitude across the direction of travel.

We demonstrate full optical control over the linear polarization state of exciton-polariton condensates, utilizing a strategy that enables polarization rotation without the need for magnetic fields. This approach leverages the intrinsic coupling between in-plane momentum and the polarization orientation of the resulting condensate. By adjusting the linear polarization of the pump laser, we can precisely dictate the condensate's angular polarization alignment. This effect persists even in scenarios involving multiple condensation sites and within the context of momentum-space superradiance.

We introduce and examine a class of Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equations featuring nonlocal terms that scale as the square of the spatial derivative. For deterministic initial data, we establish the existence of a unique global solution within a framework of Hölder spaces $C^\alpha$ for $\alpha<1$, subject to a smallness constraint on the Lipschitz constant of the initial height function. Conversely, in the context of random initial data, provided its regularity is sufficiently high, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of a unique solution which is invariant under spatial shifts and satisfies a strong Markov property.

This paper examines how readily obtainable data can guide public health responses to epidemics, utilizing South Africa's COVID-19 experience. The study employs a Bayesian framework to estimate the time-varying reproduction number ($R_t$) and cumulative infections, accounting for under-reporting. Results indicate that $R_t$ surpassed 2 early in the outbreak, peaking above 3 before declining due to containment efforts. While reported cases remained low, the authors' adjusted estimates suggest over 100,000 infections by the end of 2020. The research concludes that even basic datasets, when properly analyzed, can effectively support decision-making during pandemics.

Although Freiman's 3k-4 Theorem has been extensively studied, we offer a novel proof that provides a meaningful strengthening of the result. Specifically, we demonstrate that if the sumset of a finite set of integers, 3A, has cardinality no greater than 3|A|-4, then the set A is contained within an arithmetic progression of length at most |A|+2.

This paper introduces a novel methodology for detecting glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy by integrating multimodal clinical data, specifically fundus photographs and Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) scans. Although prior research has examined these conditions using either modularity in isolation, the combined analysis remains unexplored. Our proposed framework employs two separate ResNet models, each specialized for a particular imaging type, with their respective predictions merged using a linear fusion strategy. Evaluated on the RIM-ONE OCT dataset, this approach achieved an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.9899 for glaucoma detection and 0.9899 for diabetic retinopathy classification.

This paper introduces a novel approach for identifying potential ICU admission needs in COVID-19 patients by analyzing chest X-rays. Although current X-ray analysis primarily supports diagnosis, this study seeks to determine if they can also forecast disease progression. We trained a model to locate abnormalities within ICU admission X-rays and discovered that the model's detected regions align with findings from existing literature regarding COVID-19 X-ray patterns. Furthermore, we observed that the spatial distribution of these anomalies varies based on the severity of the patient's condition. These findings suggest that specific X-ray characteristics can indicate how severely infected individuals will become, potentially offering a valuable tool for resource allocation in healthcare settings.

This study examines transmission eigenvalues and associated eigenfunctions within spherical layered optical media. Transmission eigenvalues are identified as specific values for the scalar parameter $\lambda$ that enable a solution to the boundary value problem:
